The company, which trains robots to make and test promising compounds identified by researchers, has raised $215 million at an $865 million valuation, according to Weil, who announced the startup and funding on X. The round was led by Lightspeed, with participation from IVP, Mayfield, Lux Capital, Premji Invest, and Menlo Ventures. For years, biotech companies have outsourced the most labor-intensive work of synthesizing thousands of variations of molecules to contractors in China, such as WuXi AppTec. With Warp Sciences, Weil hopes to reshore that work and insulate the entire drug development process from geopolitical supply-chain risks. Wearing cameras and sensor gloves, the startup’s human chemists will train robots to perform various lab tasks. By automating wet-lab work, Warp Sciences aims to accelerate drug discovery using robots that can operate around the clock. Of course, you may believe otherwise if you plan to use your employer’s proprietary information to train an AI agent to do the heavy lifting for you. Seth Kugler, partner at Grellas Shah LLP. That is exactly what the defendant attempted in a recent federal trade secrets case I litigated on behalf of a client in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. In that case, the defendant, a former senior employee at the marketing agency, didn’t just copy client lists to solicit accounts. Instead, he used stolen trade secrets as training inputs to build, essentially, an AI version of his old boss, attempting a shortcut to create a competing business without spending years developing the skills and expertise typically needed to provide such services. AI is creating new ways to misappropriate trade secrets, well beyond the classic theft story of an employee downloading files onto a thumb drive. This case highlights a new reality for founders, exposing unprecedented risks related to AI and trade secrets, employee use of personal devices, and the heightened need for companies to protect themselves in the age of agentic AI. signals.title: When A Startup Sells, Its Employees’ Equity Plans Can Change Overnight
signals.description: Artificial intelligence • Job market • Liquidity • M&A When A Startup Sells, Its Employees’ Equity Plans Can Change Overnight Guest AuthorOctober 21, 2026 Guest Author 0 Shares Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn By Ron Honig Acquisitions are reshaping the technology industry. Venture-backed AI companies acquired 195 AI startups this year through late September, already exceeding the total for all of 2025, Crunchbase data shows. For investors and founders, such acquisitions can represent major financial milestones. For employees holding equity compensation, a transaction can also change personal financial plans they had expected to follow for years. A client whose employer was acquired in an all-cash transaction described to me the atmosphere inside the company during the weeks that followed: Employees repeatedly discussed the deal in office corridors, trying to understand what it meant for their equity awards, their jobs and their future. She compared the confusion to the atmosphere surrounding a major reorganization or a round of layoffs. The transaction offered the prospect of substantial financial gains. Yet employees were struggling to establish what those gains would mean for them individually. One acquisition, different outcomes Ron Honig, co-CEO of From-Honig Family Office. Employees at the same company can emerge from an acquisition with remarkably different financial outcomes. Some own vested shares. Others hold restricted stock units, stock options or performance-based awards. Their rights depend on grant agreements, vesting conditions and transaction terms. Even two employees holding RSUs may face different payment schedules or employment requirements. Depending on the agreements, outstanding awards may be settled in cash, accelerated, converted into replacement awards, or remain subject to future conditions. One employee might receive a substantial payment when the transaction closes. Another may have much of the expected value tied to continued employment.
